**Octavio Paz's "Sunstone"**
A 1957 circular poem by Mexico's Nobel laureate Octavio Paz. Its 584 lines match the 584-day cycle of Venus in the Aztec calendar, and it begins and ends with the same lines: "a willow of crystal, a poplar of water." It describes the "turning course of a river that goes curving, advances and retreats, goes roundabout, arriving forever," and contains images like "writing of fire on the slab of jade." Eliot Weinberger translated it into English, and Paz also wrote the poetry collections Eagle or Sun? and Salamander.

**The Labyrinth of Solitude**
Paz's 1950 book of essays on Mexican identity, written while he was a diplomat (he later served as Mexico's ambassador to India). It opens with an essay on the pachucos, young Mexican-Americans in Los Angeles, and discusses the "masks" Mexicans wear. Other chapters include "The Day of the Dead," "The Conquest and Colonialism," and "The Dialectic of Solitude."

**"The Sons of La Malinche"**
The most famous essay in The Labyrinth of Solitude. It analyzes the vulgar verb chingar and the figure of "la Chingada," the violated Mother, which Paz links to La Malinche, Hernán Cortés's indigenous interpreter and mistress. He contrasts this insult with the macho boast "I am your father."

**Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz's "First Dream"**
A long Baroque philosophical poem by the 17th-century nun of New Spain (colonial Mexico) known as the "Tenth Muse." It opens with a "pyramidal, funereal shadow born of the earth" as night falls and the soul tries in sleep to understand the universe. It ends at dawn with "the world illuminated and I awake."

**"You Foolish Men" and "Reply to Sor Filotea"**
In the satirical poem "You Foolish Men" ("Hombres necios"), Sor Juana attacks men who "lay the guilt on women" for faults they cause, asking who is more to blame, she who sins for pay or he who "pays to sin," and mocking men who want a Thais while courting but a Lucretia once they possess her. In her "Reply to Sor Filotea" (Philothea), she defends women's right to education and learning.

**Sor Juana, or The Traps of Faith**
Octavio Paz's 1982 biography and critical study of Sor Juana, which places her life and work in the culture of colonial New Spain.

**The Old Gringo**
A 1985 novel by Carlos Fuentes inspired by the 1913 disappearance in revolutionary Mexico of the American writer Ambrose Bierce. An aging American journalist (the "old gringo") who carries a copy of Don Quixote and wants to die joins Pancho Villa's forces. The American governess Harriet Winslow has an affair with the revolutionary General Tomás Arroyo. Arroyo shoots the gringo, and then Villa has the gringo's body dug up and shot by a firing squad, and has Arroyo executed.

**The Death of Artemio Cruz**
Fuentes's 1962 Latin American Boom novel, told in shifting first, second, and third person. It recounts the memories of Artemio Cruz, a corrupt newspaper tycoon and politician, from his deathbed. He rose from revolutionary soldier to millionaire by betraying his ideals, and he taunts his wife Catalina and daughter Teresa by refusing to say where his will is while a priest gives him last rites. The novel has been compared to Citizen Kane.

**Like Water for Chocolate**
Laura Esquivel's 1989 magical realist novel, divided into twelve monthly chapters that each begin with a recipe. Tita, the youngest daughter, is forbidden to marry her love Pedro, who marries her sister Rosaura instead. Tita's emotions pass into her cooking, so her tears in the wedding cake batter make all the guests sick. At the end, after Pedro dies, Tita eats candles and the ranch burns.

**Pedro Páramo**
Juan Rulfo's 1955 novel. Juan Preciado goes to the town of Comala to find his father, the tyrannical landowner Pedro Páramo, and finds it full of ghosts and whispering voices. Juan himself dies of fright and is buried next to Dorotea. Pedro, heartbroken over the death of Susana San Juan, lets Comala starve, and he is finally killed by his illegitimate son Abundio Martínez.

**Aura**
A short Gothic novella by Fuentes, written in the second person. The young historian Felipe Montero is hired by the ancient widow Consuelo to edit her dead husband's memoirs and falls in love with her green-eyed niece Aura, who turns out to be a magical projection of Consuelo herself.

**The Power and the Glory**
Graham Greene's 1940 novel, set in a Mexican state where the Church is outlawed. A nameless alcoholic "whiskey priest" is on the run from a lieutenant. He is sheltered by Coral Fellows in her family's barn, betrayed by a mestizo, and executed by firing squad, which the English dentist Mr. Tench watches.

**Under the Volcano**
Malcolm Lowry's 1947 novel, set in Quauhnahuac (based on Cuernavaca) on the Day of the Dead, 1938. Geoffrey Firmin, an alcoholic former British consul, is shot and thrown into a ravine, and his estranged wife Yvonne is trampled by a horse frightened by the gunshot.

**The Underdogs**
Mariano Azuela's 1915 novel of the Mexican Revolution. Demetrio Macías, a farmer turned rebel general, leads a band of fighters, and at the end he is found dead, still aiming his rifle.

**Roberto Bolaño's The Savage Detectives and 2666**
Novels by the Chilean writer Bolaño that are set largely in Mexico. In The Savage Detectives, the section "Mexicans Lost in Mexico" is the diary of a young poet who joins the Visceral Realists. In 2666, three literary critics search Mexico for the reclusive German author Benno von Archimboldi.
